claims.text: Standard EAM references exhibit configurational mismatches for equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, especially in the high-temperature liquid and near-melting solid states.
A self-consistent iterative force-matching correction applied to a standard EAM will improve reference–ab initio phase-space overlap.
The phase-space-overlap improvement will occur in both solid and liquid high-entropy-alloy states near melting.
The corrected reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately twofold relative to TOR-TILD's conventional EAM references.
The proposed method couples thermodynamic integration, ab initio recalibration, and force matching to iteratively update a refined potential.
The method is intended to apply to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi over approximately 1300–1600 K.
The range 1300–1600 K is near the melting temperature and covers both solid and liquid states of the specified alloy.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can provide force and energy data across a broad spectrum of relevant configurations.
Force matching can derive corrections from differences between ab initio outputs and conventional-EAM predictions.
Feeding force-matched corrections back into the potential will progressively make its sampled configurational phase space overlap more closely with the ab initio target.
Increasing configurational phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration mismatch.
The corrected-potential free energy will converge to within approximately 1 meV/atom of an independent ab initio benchmark.
TOR-TILD's conventional EAM-based references typically have significant discrepancies because they cannot represent the full range of many-body interactions in high-temperature disordered states.
The method is primarily applicable near melting to high-entropy alloys for which a standard EAM is available as the initial potential.
Systems with extremely strong electronic or magnetic effects may require adaptation beyond the proposed force-matching corrections.
The quantitative mismatch reduction depends on the fidelity of the ab initio training data and the iterative convergence criteria.
